newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German budget overrun makes EMU task tougher.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German budget overrun makes EMU task tougher.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday that federal government borrowing last year overshot budget targets by more than expected, making the job of qualifying for European monetary union even harder.
Final budget results for 1996 showed that new government borrowing overshot the target by 18.4 billion marks to hit 78.3 billion marks ($49 billion).

That figure was even higher than predictions Waigel had made last autumn, and put the total public sector deficit -- which includes regional states and municipalities -- at 3.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Under the Maastricht treaty, countries wanting to join in the planned launch of the euro in 1999 must reduce their total budget deficit to three percent of GDP this year.
"The budget result makes it clear how difficult a situation federal finances are in," Waigel said in a statement.

"To achieve the necessary reduction in new borrowing to fulfil the fiscal goals of the Maastricht treaty on monetary union, and to create room for tax cuts, we must continue our savings course with greater determination."

The Maastricht treaty leaves some leeway to miss the target, but both Waigel and the German Bundesbank have insisted on hitting the goal exactly to ensure that the euro is as strong a currency as the mark.
That will not be easy to achieve. Although federal spending, at 455.6 billion marks, overshot spending targets by only 4.3 billion, the real problem was on the revenue side.
Federal tax income was 12.6 percent below plan at 338.6 billion marks.

Waigel blamed last year's "unfavourable result" on the fact that economic growth fell far short of expectations. Gross domestic product rose by just 1.4 percent, against forecasts of 2.0-2.5 percent on which last year's budget was based.
German economists said there were risks that the assumptions underlying Waigel's 1997 budget -- of 2.5 percent growth and unemployment below four million -- were too optimistic.

Unemployment in December hit a post-war record 4.1 million and is set to top 4.5 million this winter. Most forecasters see the figure averaging above four million this year, straining the state jobless benefits budget.

But, the economists said, a cross-party consensus in Germany on the need to lead monetary union from the front would mean that Waigel would manage to keep the total deficit to three percent of GDP this year.
"There is no alternative to the consolidation course," said Peter Pietsch at Commerzbank in Frankfurt. "I am convinced that we will achieve this goal because the political will is there."
Ralf Kugelstadt at UBS Global Research agreed: "We still have a forecast of three percent. But the risks are still there from the labour market."

Although some economists see slower economic growth this year than officially forecast, they said that even two percent growth would give Waigel enough leeway to contain borrowing sufficiently by clamping down on federal spending.
They did not expect a restrictive fiscal policy to dampen economic activity so much that the revenue side of the German fiscal equation would be hit.
"When I do my calculations, I get a deficit of three percent," Gerhard Grebe of Bank Julius Baer said.
